title: Solids, Liquids and Gases
seo_title: Grade 4 Natural Sciences and Technology: Solids, Liquids and Gases Worksheets (CAPS)
standard_code: Grade 4 Natural Sciences and Technology: Materials around us
standard_text: Materials can be solids, liquids or gases. Solids keep their shape, liquids flow and take the shape of their container, and gases spread out to fill a space. Materials can be raw (natural) or manufactured, and materials and shapes can be strengthened. (summary of CAPS Natural Sciences and Technology, Grade 4, Matter and Materials: Materials around us)
meta_desc: Free Grade 4 Natural Sciences and Technology worksheets (CAPS): properties of solids, liquids and gases, raw and manufactured materials, and strengthening materials. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: Solids keep their shape; liquids flow; gases spread out.
key_sub: Folding, rolling and tubes make materials stronger.
body_html:
How to think about it

A solid keeps its own shape (a brick). A liquid flows and takes the shape of its container, but keeps its volume (water). A gas spreads out to fill all the space it is in (air in a balloon).

Raw materials come from nature (wood, clay, wool); manufactured materials are made by people (plastic, glass, paper). Paper becomes stronger when it is folded, rolled into a tube or made into a triangle shape.

Example

Sand can be poured. Is it a liquid?

Look at one grain.

Answer: no, each grain is a solid

Example

Which is stronger: a flat sheet of paper or a paper tube?

Think of a drinking straw.

Answer: the paper tube

Common mistakes

  • Thinking sand or sugar is a liquid because it pours.
  • Thinking gases have no mass.
  • Thinking all manufactured materials are better than raw ones.

faq.q: Is toothpaste a solid or a liquid?
faq.a: It is a thick mixture; it flows slowly like a liquid when you squeeze it.

faq.q: Why are bridges built with triangles?
faq.a: Triangles do not change shape easily, so they make strong frames.

items.q: In which state are the particles close together but able to slide past each other?
items.e: Everything is made of tiny particles.

items.q: In which state are the particles packed closely in a regular pattern, vibrating on the spot?
items.e: Everything is made of tiny particles.

items.q: Is oxygen a solid, a liquid or a gas?
items.e: Oxygen is a gas.

items.q: Which states of matter cannot be squashed into a smaller space?
items.e: Solids keep their shape; liquids flow; gases spread out and can be squashed.

items.q: How are the particles arranged in a gas?
c: packed closely in a regular pattern, vibrating on the spot
far apart and moving quickly in all directions
close together but able to slide past each other
items.e: Everything is made of tiny particles.

items.q: Which state of matter can be squashed into a smaller space?
items.e: Solids keep their shape; liquids flow; gases spread out and can be squashed.

items.e: Solids keep their shape; liquids flow; gases spread out and can be squashed.

items.q: Is sugar a solid, a liquid or a gas?
items.e: Each grain is a solid; the grains pour.

items.q: Is air a solid, a liquid or a gas?
items.e: Air is a gas.

items.q: In which state are the particles far apart and moving quickly in all directions?

items.q: Is melted chocolate a solid, a liquid or a gas?
items.e: Melted chocolate is a liquid.

items.q: Which of these is a solid: flour, helium in a balloon, milk or the bubbles in a fizzy drink?

items.e: Tiny solid grains pour, but each keeps its shape.

items.q: Which of these is a gas: a wooden spoon, melted chocolate, oxygen or shampoo?
items.e: Oxygen is a gas.

items.q: Which of these is a solid: a coin, milk, the air inside a soccer or the bubbles in a fizzy drink?
c: the bubbles in a fizzy drink
items.e: A coin is a solid.

items.q: Is carbon dioxide a solid, a liquid or a gas?
items.e: Carbon dioxide is a gas.

items.q: How are the particles arranged in a liquid?

far apart and moving quickly in all directions
close together but able to slide past each other
items.e: Everything is made of tiny particles.

items.q: Which of these is a liquid: a wooden spoon, sugar, the bubbles in a fizzy drink or vinegar?
c: the bubbles in a fizzy drink
items.e: Vinegar is a liquid.

items.q: Which state of matter keeps the same volume but changes shape?
items.e: Solids keep their shape; liquids flow; gases spread out and can be squashed.

items.q: Which state of matter spreads out to fill any container?
items.e: Solids keep their shape; liquids flow; gases spread out and can be squashed.

items.q: Which of these is a solid: a wooden spoon, air, shampoo or water?
items.e: A wooden spoon is a solid.

items.q: What does diagram A show?
c: a gas: particles far apart, moving quickly in all directions
a liquid: particles close together but jumbled, sliding past each other
a solid: particles close together in a regular pattern, vibrating on the spot
a gas: particles packed tightly in rows
items.e: Solids: regular pattern. Liquids: close but jumbled. Gases: far apart.

items.q: What is all matter made of?
c: tiny particles that are too small to see
items.e: Solids, liquids and gases are all made of particles.

items.q: Do the particles in a solid move?
c: Yes, they vibrate on the spot.
Only when the solid is cold.
Yes, they move freely around the room.
items.e: They vibrate but stay in place.

items.q: Liquids have a fixed volume but take the shape of their container. Which idea about particles explains this?
c: the particles are far apart and move freely
the particles are held in fixed places
the particles are close but can slide past each other
items.e: Particle model: liquids, because the particles are close but can slide past each other.

items.q: Solids can be held in your hand and do not flow. Which idea about particles explains this?
c: the particles are held in fixed places
the particles are far apart and move freely
the particles are close but can slide past each other
items.e: Particle model: solids, because the particles are held in fixed places.

items.q: What does diagram B show?
c: a liquid: particles close together but jumbled, sliding past each other
a gas: particles packed tightly in rows
a solid: particles close together in a regular pattern, vibrating on the spot
a gas: particles far apart, moving quickly in all directions
items.e: Solids: regular pattern. Liquids: close but jumbled. Gases: far apart.

items.q: Which diagram shows the particles in water in a glass?
c: none of them: water in a glass has no particles
items.e: Ice is a solid, liquid water is a liquid, water vapour is a gas.

items.q: Gases can be squashed (compressed) easily. Which idea about particles explains this?
c: the particles are close but can slide past each other
the particles are held in fixed places
the particles are far apart and move freely
items.e: Particle model: gases, because the particles are far apart and move freely.

items.q: Which diagram shows the particles in ice?
c: none of them: ice has no particles
items.e: Ice is a solid, liquid water is a liquid, water vapour is a gas.

items.q: Gases spread out to fill any container. Which idea about particles explains this?
c: the particles are far apart and move freely
the particles are close but can slide past each other
the particles are held in fixed places
items.e: Particle model: gases, because the particles are far apart and move freely.

items.q: What happens to particles when a solid is heated?
c: They vibrate faster and move further apart.
items.e: Heating gives the particles more energy.

items.q: Is sand a solid or a liquid?
c: a liquid, because it can be poured
a solid: each grain keeps its shape
items.e: Tiny solid grains can be poured, but each grain is solid.

items.q: Which diagram shows the particles in water vapour (steam)?
c: none of them: water vapour has no particles
items.e: Ice is a solid, liquid water is a liquid, water vapour is a gas.

items.q: What does diagram C show?
c: a solid: particles close together in a regular pattern, vibrating on the spot
a liquid: particles close together but jumbled, sliding past each other
a solid: particles far apart and not moving
a gas: particles far apart, moving quickly in all directions
items.e: Solids: regular pattern. Liquids: close but jumbled. Gases: far apart.

items.q: A bike tyre is pumped up. Where do the extra air particles go?
c: They are squashed closer together inside the tyre.
items.e: Gases can be compressed.

items.q: Solids keep their own shape. Which idea about particles explains this?
c: the particles are far apart and move freely
the particles are close but can slide past each other
the particles are held in fixed places
items.e: Particle model: solids, because the particles are held in fixed places.

items.q: What does diagram A show?
c: a gas: particles far apart, moving quickly in all directions
a liquid: particles close together but jumbled, sliding past each other
a solid: particles close together in a regular pattern, vibrating on the spot
a gas: particles packed tightly in rows
items.e: Solids: regular pattern. Liquids: close but jumbled. Gases: far apart.

items.q: Which diagram shows the particles in water in a glass?
c: none of them: water in a glass has no particles
items.e: Ice is a solid, liquid water is a liquid, water vapour is a gas.

items.q: Which state of matter can be poured but cannot be compressed easily?
items.e: Solids: definite shape and volume. Liquids: definite volume, no definite shape. Gases: no definite shape or volume.

items.q: Which of these is NOT matter?
items.e: A thought has no mass and does not occupy space.

items.q: A deflated ball has a mass of 400 g. After it is pumped with air, its mass is 405 g. What does this show?
items.e: The extra mass is the mass of the air pumped in.

items.q: Which state of matter has a definite shape?
items.e: Solids: definite shape and volume. Liquids: definite volume, no definite shape. Gases: no definite shape or volume.

items.q: Which of these is matter?
items.e: Water has mass and occupies space.

items.q: Is liquid soap a solid, a liquid or a gas?
items.e: It has a definite volume but no definite shape.

items.q: An empty cup has a mass of 40 g. When it is filled with sand, the mass is 90 g. What is the mass of the sand?
Which of these is NOT matter?
items.e: Sound has no mass and does not occupy space.

items.q: Is water vapour a solid, a liquid or a gas?
items.e: It has no definite shape and no definite volume.

items.q: An empty cup has a mass of 25 g. 100 g of cooking oil is put into it. What will the balance show?
Which of these is matter?
items.e: A coin has mass and occupies space.

items.q: Which of these is a liquid?
items.e: A liquid has a definite volume but no definite shape.

items.q: Which state of matter keeps its shape when moved from a bowl to a plate?
items.e: Solids: definite shape and volume. Liquids: definite volume, no definite shape. Gases: no definite shape or volume.

items.q: Which of these is matter?
items.e: An ice cube has mass and occupies space.

items.q: An empty cup has a mass of 30 g. 100 g of rice grains is put into it. What will the balance show?
Which state of matter has a definite volume?
items.e: Solids: definite shape and volume. Liquids: definite volume, no definite shape. Gases: no definite shape or volume.

items.q: Is the gas in a balloon a solid, a liquid or a gas?
items.e: It has no definite shape and no definite volume.

items.q: Which state of matter takes the shape of its container?
items.e: Solids: definite shape and volume. Liquids: definite volume, no definite shape. Gases: no definite shape or volume.

items.q: An empty cup has a mass of 20 g. When it is filled with water, the mass is 120 g. What is the mass of the water?
Which of these is a gas?
items.e: A gas has no definite shape and no definite volume.

items.q: Which of these is usually made of glass: a T-shirt, a lunchbox, a toy brick or a vase?
items.e: Think about what each object is made of.

items.q: Is leather a natural material or a made material?

items.q: Which natural material is aluminium foil mainly made from?
items.e: Aluminium foil is made from bauxite (a rock).

items.q: Is stone a natural material or a made material?
items.e: Natural materials are found in nature and used with little change.

items.q: Which of these is usually made of fabric: a comb, a curtain, a drinks bottle or a lunchbox?
items.e: Think about what each object is made of.

items.q: Is clay a natural material or a made material?
items.e: Natural materials are found in nature and used with little change.

items.q: Which natural material is steel mainly made from?
items.e: Steel is made from iron ore.

items.q: Which of these is usually made of paper: a drinks bottle, a newspaper, a toy brick or a wooden spoon?
items.e: Think about what each object is made of.

items.q: Is a coat an object or a material?

items.q: Which of these is usually made of paper: a T-shirt, a birthday card, a drinks bottle or a pillowcase?
items.e: Think about what each object is made of.

items.q: Which property makes glass good for windows?

items.q: What is a natural material?
c: a material made in a factory
a material found in nature, such as wood, wool or stone
items.e: Natural materials come from plants, animals or the ground.

items.q: Is glass a natural material or a made material?
items.e: Made (processed) materials are made by people by changing natural materials, such as glass from sand.

items.q: Which natural material is nylon mainly made from?
items.e: Nylon is made from oil.

items.q: Is metal an object or a material?
items.e: An object is a thing. A material is what the thing is made of.

items.q: Why are bricks used to build houses?
c: They are strong, hard and do not burn easily.
items.e: Choose materials by their properties.

items.q: Is water an object or a material?
items.e: An object is a thing. A material is what the thing is made of.

items.q: Why is rubber used for car tyres?
c: It is flexible, tough and grips the road.
items.e: Rubber bends without breaking.

items.q: Is a window an object or a material?
items.e: An object is a thing. A material is what the thing is made of.

items.q: Sarah takes apart a necklace. What will Sarah find?

items.e: Big objects are made of smaller pieces.

items.q: Which is the strongest way to join two craft sticks?

items.q: Why are snow forts built with thick walls at the bottom?
c: Thick bottoms hold the weight of the snow above.

items.q: Lindiwe takes apart a toy car. What will Lindiwe find?

items.e: Big objects are made of smaller pieces.

items.q: Which is a natural structure?

items.q: Elna takes apart a sandwich. What will Elna find?

items.e: Big objects are made of smaller pieces.

items.q: Liam built a house with 29 blocks. He took it apart and used all the blocks to build a train. How many blocks are in the train?

items.q: Why do bridges over wide rivers often have many pillars?

items.e: Supports share the load.

items.q: What is the job of a pillar or column?

to make a building taller only

items.q: Elna takes apart a paper chain. What will Elna find?

items.q: Which material is best for building a strong bridge for a toy car?

items.q: Kabelo built a car with 19 blocks. He took it apart and used all the blocks to build a dog. How many blocks are in the dog?

items.q: Why are glass windows thick in tall buildings?

items.q: Daniel built a car with 22 blocks. He took it apart and used all the blocks to build a bridge. How many blocks are in the bridge?
